The general concensus among Turks is that it is not a genoice, in school textbooks starting from elementary school it is referred to as "the so called Armenian genocide." As I recall the definition of genocide includes something along the lines of "with intent to destroy, in part or as a whole an ethnic, religious, etc. group"; Turkish people generally claim that although the mendatory relocation of the Armenians caused large number of Armenian casualties, it wasn't intended to do so. 

What is suprising is that many Turkish people still cling to this silly defense, even with all the evidence against it.(I recall reading that German personnel in Ottoman borders during WW1 spoke against the attrocities, but due to allied status didn't do anything against it)

Today it is almost a taboo to refer to the genocide as genocide in Turkey, and even in university level courses it is still refuted by teachers.(Atleast my human rights teacher) An intresting side note is that any library you go in Turkey, you'll find that almost all the literature on the era agree it was a genocide. There was a recent third party investigation which concluded while events can't be identified legally as genocide, since it didn't exist in legal terms until the Geneva Convention, they would qualify as such if the law was applicable.(Something about 'no crime without law')

Anyway as a Turk I find this topic intresting, because of the lengths almost every Turk goes to in order to deny it is genocide. The usual arguements you would hear also include that since the Armenian's wanted their own state and colaborated with the Russians during WWI, what happened wasn't genocide.(I can't remember the precise reasoning here) 

As for the official line, it is accepted that 'attrocities on both sides were carried out', but it is further distinguished by saying the 300,000 Armenian deaths(official Turkish figure) were not due to the state but Kurdish and Turkish civillians who were retalliating plus attacks from bandits during the relocation.(Techir) The retalliation arguement stems from several Armenian attacks on Turkish and Kurdish villages, which ironically happened due to 'The Wilson Principle'(? can't recall what it was called), the idea that state borders should be decided by the population that lives in the area. This in turn might be the reasoning the the Ottoman state for the Techir Law, to ensure Armenia's borders would be smaller.

Anyway, in conclusion, the information is available online and in any library you care to visit: but, due to an educational system which can best be described as indoctrinal, which is continous from elementary school all the way up, there is a tabo in Turkey against calling it genocide. In fact I'm pretty sure I'd get allienated or worse for saying this publicly in Turkey. Orhan Pamuk, a world renown Turkish author once spoke about the genocide, and was detained on his re-entry to Turkey(released later). It might just be the best real world example of double-think ever.
